title: Somatosensation & Pain
summary: How touch, position, temperature and pain reach awareness.

lessons.title: Receptors & Fiber Types

levels.kid:
Your skin is full of tiny helpers called receptors. Each one listens for a different thing.

Some feel a soft touch, like a feather. Some feel buzzing, like a phone vibrating. Some feel hot or cold. Some feel "ouch!"

When a helper feels something, it sends a message up a nerve wire to your brain.

Some wires are thick and wrapped in a coat, so their messages zoom super fast. Others are thin with no coat, so they are slow.

That is why when you stub your toe, you feel a quick sharp ouch first, and then a slow, achy ouch a second later!
levels.hs:
Somatosensation is the body's sense of touch, body position (proprioception), temperature and pain. It starts with **sensory receptors**, the endings of sensory neurons whose cell bodies sit in the **dorsal root ganglia** next to the spinal cord.

Skin has four main touch receptors:
- **Meissner corpuscles**: light touch and flutter, very sensitive in fingertips
- **Merkel discs**: steady pressure and texture
- **Pacinian corpuscles**: vibration, deep in the skin
- **Ruffini endings**: skin stretch

Muscles have **muscle spindles** (sense muscle length) and tendons have **Golgi tendon organs** (sense muscle tension). Together they tell your brain where your limbs are without looking.

Pain and temperature come from **free nerve endings**, bare branches of thin nerve fibers.

Fiber size matters. Thick, myelinated fibers (**A-beta**) carry touch fast. Thin, lightly myelinated **A-delta** fibers carry sharp "first pain" and cold. Thin, unmyelinated **C fibers** carry slow, burning "second pain," warmth and itch.

So stubbing a toe gives a sharp jab (A-delta) followed by a dull throb (C fibers).
levels.college:
**Primary afferents** are pseudounipolar neurons with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia (or trigeminal ganglion for the face). One axon branch goes to the periphery; the other enters the spinal cord.

**Mechanoreceptors** differ in adaptation and receptive field size:
- Meissner corpuscles: rapidly adapting, small fields, flutter and slip detection
- Merkel cell complexes: slowly adapting, small fields, form and texture
- Pacinian corpuscles: rapidly adapting, large fields, high-frequency vibration
- Ruffini endings: slowly adapting, large fields, skin stretch
Rapidly adapting receptors signal change; slowly adapting receptors signal sustained stimuli.

**Proprioceptors**: muscle spindles (intrafusal fibers; group Ia and II afferents) encode length and velocity of stretch; Golgi tendon organs (group Ib) encode tension. Joint receptors contribute mostly at extremes of range.

**Fiber classification** (Erlanger-Gasser letters; Lloyd-Hunt numerals for muscle afferents):
- A-alpha (Ia, Ib): largest, fastest; proprioception
- A-beta (II): touch and vibration
- A-delta (III): sharp pain, cold
- C (IV): unmyelinated, slowest; burning pain, warmth, itch
Conduction velocity rises with diameter and myelination.

**Transduction** uses specific ion channels: **Piezo2** for touch and proprioception, **TRPV1** for noxious heat and capsaicin, **TRPM8** for cold and menthol, **TRPA1** for chemical irritants.

**Receptive field density** determines acuity: two-point discrimination is a few millimeters at the fingertip but several centimeters on the back, matching receptor density and cortical magnification.
levels.phd:
Somatosensory coding begins with molecularly defined afferent classes. Single-cell RNA sequencing of dorsal root ganglia has split the classical categories into many transcriptomic types: several low-threshold mechanoreceptor (LTMR) classes (A-beta rapidly adapting, A-beta slowly adapting type I with Merkel cells, A-delta LTMRs around hair follicles, C-LTMRs signaling pleasant, slow stroking), multiple peptidergic and non-peptidergic nociceptor classes, and pruriceptors.

**Mechanotransduction.** Piezo2 is the principal mechanically activated channel in LTMRs and proprioceptors. Humans with loss-of-function PIEZO2 mutations have severe deficits in discriminative touch and proprioception, yet can still walk using vision, a striking demonstration that proprioception is largely Piezo2-dependent. Merkel cells themselves express Piezo2 and help shape slowly adapting responses.

**Nociceptor excitability.** Voltage-gated sodium channels Nav1.7, Nav1.8 and Nav1.9 are enriched in nociceptors. Nav1.7 sets the threshold: loss-of-function mutations in SCN9A cause congenital insensitivity to pain (with anosmia), whereas gain-of-function mutations cause inherited erythromelalgia and paroxysmal extreme pain disorder. This human genetics made Nav1.7 a prime analgesic target, though selective blockers have struggled clinically, partly because of the role of endogenous opioid upregulation in the null phenotype.

**Silent nociceptors** are mechanically insensitive C fibers that become responsive during inflammation, contributing to hyperalgesia.

**Coding principles.** Labeled-line theory (each fiber class encodes one quality) competes with population coding (quality emerges from patterns across classes). Itch illustrates the debate: dedicated pruriceptors and spinal gastrin-releasing peptide circuits support labeled lines, while cross-inhibition between pain and itch pathways shows interaction. Most evidence now supports specialized lines with substantial convergence and modulation in the dorsal horn.
levels.expert:
**Why fiber types matter at the bedside.** Your sensory exam is a fiber-type exam. Vibration and joint position test large myelinated fibers (A-beta, group Ia, II) and the dorsal columns. Pinprick and temperature test small fibers (A-delta, C) and the spinothalamic system.

**Large-fiber vs small-fiber neuropathy:**
- Large-fiber: lost vibration and proprioception, sensory ataxia, positive Romberg, reduced reflexes. Nerve conduction studies are abnormal.
- Small-fiber: burning feet, allodynia, lost pinprick and temperature, often autonomic symptoms; strength, reflexes and **nerve conduction studies are normal**, because NCS only measures large myelinated fibers.
- Diagnose small-fiber neuropathy with **skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fiber density**, or autonomic testing (QSART). A normal NCS does not rule out neuropathy in a patient with burning feet.

**Differential block.** Local anesthetics block small fibers early, so pain and temperature disappear before touch and motor function. Compression and ischemia hit large myelinated fibers first, which is why a leg "falling asleep" loses touch and position sense before pain.

**Genetic pain syndromes** to recognize: SCN9A (Nav1.7) gain-of-function causes erythromelalgia (burning red feet worse with heat); loss-of-function causes congenital insensitivity to pain, presenting as painless injuries, burns and joint destruction in children.

**Surgical relevance.** The dorsal root carries afferents into the cord; a dorsal rhizotomy abolishes sensation from that root, while a ganglion lesion also removes the cell body. Intraoperative somatosensory evoked potentials depend on large-fiber afferents, so they monitor dorsal column function but say nothing about pain pathways.

Pitfall: sensory symptoms that do not fit any fiber type, nerve, root or central pattern should prompt you to re-examine carefully before labeling them non-organic.

keyPoints: Primary afferent cell bodies sit in the dorsal root ganglia (trigeminal ganglion for the face)
Meissner = light touch/flutter, Merkel = pressure/texture, Pacinian = vibration, Ruffini = stretch
Muscle spindles sense length (Ia, II); Golgi tendon organs sense tension (Ib)
A-beta = touch; A-delta = sharp first pain and cold; C = slow burning pain, warmth, itch
Piezo2 transduces touch/proprioception; TRPV1 heat; TRPM8 cold
Nerve conduction studies only measure large myelinated fibers

test.q: Which receptor detects high-frequency vibration?
test.explain: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting, deep receptors tuned to vibration. Merkel discs sense sustained pressure and texture.

test.q: Muscle spindles mainly sense:
test.explain: Spindles sit parallel to muscle fibers and encode length and velocity of stretch. Golgi tendon organs sense tension.

test.q: Which fibers carry slow, burning 'second pain'?
test.explain: Unmyelinated C fibers conduct slowly and carry dull, burning pain. A-delta fibers carry the fast, sharp first pain.

test.q: Where are the cell bodies of spinal sensory neurons?
test.explain: Primary afferents are pseudounipolar neurons with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia.

test.q: A rapidly adapting receptor mainly signals:
choices: Changes such as onset, offset and vibration
test.explain: Rapidly adapting receptors fire at stimulus change; slowly adapting ones keep firing during sustained stimuli.

test.q: The capsaicin (chili pepper) receptor TRPV1 is also activated by:
test.explain: TRPV1 responds to noxious heat and capsaicin, which is why chilies feel hot. Cold and menthol act on TRPM8.

test.q: Why do A-beta fibers conduct faster than C fibers?
test.explain: Larger diameter and myelin (saltatory conduction) both increase conduction velocity.

test.q: Two-point discrimination is best on the:
test.explain: Fingertips have dense small receptive fields and a large cortical representation.

test.q: Golgi tendon organs sense muscle ___.
test.explain: They are in series with the muscle at the tendon and are innervated by group Ib afferents.

test.q: Name the unmyelinated pain fiber type (one letter).
test.explain: C fibers are unmyelinated and slow; they carry burning pain, warmth and itch.

test.q: The ion channel ___ is the main mechanotransducer for touch and proprioception.
test.explain: Humans lacking Piezo2 have severe loss of discriminative touch and proprioception.

test.q: Which receptor senses light touch and flutter in fingertips? (two words)
test.explain: Meissner corpuscles are rapidly adapting with small receptive fields in glabrous skin.

kidTest.q: What do receptors in your skin do?
choices: Feel things like touch and heat
kidTest.explain: Receptors are tiny helpers that feel touch, buzzing, heat, cold and pain.

kidTest.q: Thick nerve wires with a coat send messages:
kidTest.explain: The coat (myelin) and the thickness make messages zoom fast.

kidTest.q: When you stub your toe, what do you feel first?
kidTest.explain: The fast wires bring the sharp ouch first; the slow wires bring the ache after.

kidTest.q: Which helper feels buzzing, like a phone vibrating?
kidTest.explain: Special receptors deep in the skin feel vibration.

kidTest.q: Messages from your skin travel up nerves to your ___.
kidTest.explain: The brain is where you notice the feeling.

kidTest.q: Thin wires with no coat are:
kidTest.explain: No coat and thin means slow messages, like the achy pain.

advancedTest.q: A patient has burning feet, reduced pinprick sensation, normal strength and reflexes, and a normal nerve conduction study. Best next test?
choices: Skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fiber density
advancedTest.explain: This is small-fiber neuropathy. NCS measures only large myelinated fibers; skin biopsy quantifies small fibers.
Nav1.7 sets nociceptor threshold. Loss of function abolishes pain; gain of function causes erythromelalgia and paroxysmal extreme pain disorder.

advancedTest.q: A leg 'falls asleep' from compression. Which sensation is typically lost first?
advancedTest.explain: Compression and ischemia affect large myelinated fibers first; local anesthetics tend to block small fibers first.

advancedTest.q: Which receptor class encodes muscle length via group Ia afferents? (two words)
advancedTest.explain: Spindles carry Ia (velocity and length) and II (length) afferents.

lessons.title: Touch & Proprioception Pathways

levels.kid:
Close your eyes and touch your nose. How did you find it? Your body has a secret sense that knows where your arms and legs are!

Messages about touch and body position ride up a special road in the back of your spinal cord. It is like a fast highway.

At the bottom of your brain, the road crosses over to the other side. So your left hand talks to the right side of your brain!

Then the message stops at a relay station in the middle of the brain, and finally reaches a strip on top of the brain that feels touch. That strip has a little map of your whole body.
levels.hs:
Fine touch, vibration and **proprioception** (knowing where your body parts are) travel in the **dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway** (DCML).

The route uses three neurons:
- **1st neuron**: sensory neuron with its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion. Its axon enters the spinal cord and climbs up the **dorsal columns** on the **same side**. Leg fibers run in the **fasciculus gracilis** (medial); arm fibers in the **fasciculus cuneatus** (lateral).
- **2nd neuron**: in the **nucleus gracilis or cuneatus** in the lower medulla. Its axon **crosses** to the other side and rises as the **medial lemniscus**.
- **3rd neuron**: in the **thalamus** (VPL nucleus), projecting to the **primary somatosensory cortex** in the postcentral gyrus.

The cortex holds a body map, the **sensory homunculus**: legs near the midline at the top, face and hands on the side. Lips and fingers get huge areas because they are so sensitive.

Face touch uses the trigeminal nerve and ends in a different thalamic nucleus (VPM).

The **Romberg test** checks proprioception: stand with feet together and close your eyes. If you sway or fall only with eyes closed, your dorsal columns (or sensory nerves) may be damaged.
levels.college:
**DCML pathway (discriminative touch, vibration, conscious proprioception):**
- First-order neurons: DRG cells whose central axons ascend **ipsilaterally** in the dorsal columns. Fibers from below about T6 form the medial **fasciculus gracilis**; above T6 they add laterally as the **fasciculus cuneatus**.
- Second-order neurons: **nucleus gracilis and cuneatus** in the caudal medulla. Their axons sweep across as **internal arcuate fibers**, decussate, and ascend as the **medial lemniscus**.
- Third-order neurons: **ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus** of the thalamus, projecting through the **posterior limb of the internal capsule** to the **primary somatosensory cortex (S1)**, Brodmann areas 3a, 3b, 1 and 2.

**Face**: trigeminal afferents synapse in the **principal (main) sensory nucleus** in the pons, cross, and ascend in the trigeminal lemniscus to the **VPM** nucleus.

**S1 organization**: area 3a receives proprioceptive input, 3b cutaneous input, area 1 texture, area 2 size, shape and integrated position. The homunculus places the leg on the medial surface (paracentral lobule, anterior cerebral artery territory) and the face and hand laterally (middle cerebral artery territory).

**Unconscious proprioception** reaches the cerebellum, not awareness: the **dorsal spinocerebellar tract** (from Clarke's nucleus, roughly C8 to L2) and the **cuneocerebellar tract** (from the accessory cuneate nucleus) travel ipsilaterally through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

**Clinical lesions:**
- Dorsal columns: vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration), tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis), copper deficiency. Positive Romberg, sensory ataxia.
- Hemisection (Brown-Séquard): ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception below the lesion.
- Medial medullary syndrome: contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration (medial lemniscus) with contralateral hemiparesis and ipsilateral tongue weakness.
- Parietal cortex: astereognosis, agraphesthesia, impaired two-point discrimination.
levels.phd:
**Beyond the textbook dorsal column.** The classical view of the dorsal columns as a pure relay of primary afferents is incomplete. A substantial component is the **postsynaptic dorsal column pathway**, arising from dorsal horn neurons, which carries visceral nociceptive information. Midline myelotomy, a small lesion of the medial dorsal columns, relieves visceral cancer pain, showing that the dorsal columns are not only a touch pathway.

**Dorsal column nuclei as processors.** The gracile and cuneate nuclei contain inhibitory interneurons and receive descending cortical input, enabling surround inhibition and gating of tactile signals during movement (sensory suppression). Recent work shows these nuclei integrate direct LTMR input with indirect input from the dorsal horn's LTMR recipient zone, producing mixed response properties.

**Cortical hierarchy.** S1 subareas form a hierarchy: 3b neurons have small receptive fields on single digits; areas 1 and 2 have larger multi-digit fields with orientation and motion selectivity. Area 2 combines cutaneous and proprioceptive inputs to encode object shape held in the hand. Information then flows to S2 in the parietal operculum and posterior parietal cortex (areas 5 and 7) for tactile object recognition and sensorimotor integration.

**Plasticity.** Merzenich and colleagues showed that after digit amputation or syndactyly in monkeys, S1 maps reorganize within weeks. In humans, the face area can invade the deafferented hand area after amputation, offering one explanation for referred phantom sensations evoked by touching the face.

**Tract somatotopy and sparing.** In the dorsal columns, sacral fibers are most medial and cervical most lateral. Compression from a posterior extradural mass may preferentially affect specific fibers, and lesions of the cuneate fasciculus at cervical levels can give arm-predominant proprioceptive loss with a pseudoathetotic "useless hand" in multiple sclerosis or cervical spondylosis.
levels.expert:
**Localizing a sensory complaint.** Ask what modality is lost, where, and on which side relative to motor signs.

- **Peripheral nerve or root**: loss in a nerve or dermatomal distribution.
- **Polyneuropathy**: length-dependent stocking-and-glove loss.
- **Spinal cord**: a **sensory level**. Dorsal column involvement gives lost vibration and joint position below the lesion, Lhermitte sign (electric shock down the spine on neck flexion, classic in cervical MS or myelopathy), and sensory ataxia.
- **Brainstem**: medial medullary lesions affect the medial lemniscus contralaterally.
- **Thalamus (VPL/VPM)**: contralateral hemisensory loss of all modalities including the face, sometimes followed weeks later by central post-stroke pain.
- **Cortex**: primary modalities relatively intact but **cortical sensory** functions fail: stereognosis, graphesthesia, two-point discrimination, and extinction to double simultaneous stimulation.

**Romberg done properly.** Feet together, arms by the sides, stable with eyes open, then eyes closed. A positive test means instability that appears or worsens markedly with eyes closed and points to proprioceptive loss (dorsal columns or large-fiber neuropathy). Cerebellar patients are unstable with eyes open too.

**Subacute combined degeneration**: B12 deficiency damages dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, so you see lost vibration plus upgoing toes, sometimes with absent ankle jerks from coexisting neuropathy. Copper deficiency (after bariatric surgery, excess zinc) mimics it.

**In the operating room.** Somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) stimulate a peripheral nerve and record over the cortex; they monitor the dorsal column pathway during spine and posterior fossa surgery. They do not monitor motor tracts, so motor evoked potentials are added, since an anterior spinal artery injury can paralyze a patient while SSEPs stay normal.

**Pitfall**: a patient with "numb hands" and clumsiness may have cervical myelopathy, not carpal tunnel. Check reflexes and Hoffmann sign before ordering wrist studies.

keyPoints: DCML carries fine touch, vibration and conscious proprioception
1st neuron ascends ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns (gracilis = legs, medial; cuneatus = arms, lateral)
2nd neuron in nucleus gracilis/cuneatus crosses in the medulla and ascends in the medial lemniscus
3rd neuron in VPL thalamus projects to S1 in the postcentral gyrus (face: VPM)
Unconscious proprioception goes ipsilaterally to the cerebellum via spinocerebellar tracts
Positive Romberg = proprioceptive (sensory) ataxia, e.g., B12 deficiency or tabes dorsalis

test.q: Where does the DCML pathway cross the midline?
choices: At the spinal level of entry
test.explain: Second-order axons from the nucleus gracilis and cuneatus decussate as internal arcuate fibers in the caudal medulla.

test.q: Leg proprioception ascends in the:
test.explain: Gracilis (medial) carries input from the legs and lower trunk; cuneatus (lateral) from the arms.

test.q: The thalamic relay for body touch is the:
test.explain: VPL handles the body; VPM the face; LGN vision; MGN hearing.

test.q: A right-sided spinal cord hemisection at T8 causes loss of vibration sense:
test.explain: Dorsal column fibers ascend ipsilaterally, so vibration and proprioception are lost on the same side below the lesion.

test.q: Primary somatosensory cortex is in the:
test.explain: S1 is in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe; motor cortex is precentral.

test.q: A patient sways and nearly falls only when closing the eyes with feet together. This suggests:
test.explain: A positive Romberg sign indicates proprioceptive (sensory) ataxia, as in dorsal column disease or large-fiber neuropathy.

test.q: Which deficiency classically damages the dorsal columns?
test.explain: B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts.

test.q: Unconscious proprioception from the legs reaches the cerebellum via the:
test.explain: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract arises from Clarke's nucleus and enters the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle on the same side.

test.q: After crossing in the medulla, DCML fibers ascend as the medial ___.
test.explain: The medial lemniscus carries crossed touch and proprioception to the VPL thalamus.

test.q: Inability to identify an object by touch alone (e.g., a key in the hand) is called?
test.explain: Astereognosis with intact primary sensation points to parietal cortex.

test.q: Fine touch from the face synapses in the trigeminal main sensory nucleus and relays in the thalamic nucleus ___.
test.explain: VPM = ventral posteromedial nucleus, the face relay.

test.q: Name the test: feet together, eyes closed, watch for swaying.
test.explain: The Romberg test detects proprioceptive loss.

kidTest.q: Which sense tells you where your arms are with your eyes closed?
kidTest.explain: Proprioception is your secret body position sense.

kidTest.q: Touch messages ride up which part of the spinal cord?
kidTest.explain: They travel in the back part, called the dorsal columns.

kidTest.q: Your left hand talks mostly to which side of your brain?
kidTest.explain: The road crosses over, so left talks to right.

kidTest.q: The strip on top of the brain that feels touch has a:
kidTest.explain: It has a little body map called the homunculus.

kidTest.q: Close your eyes and touch your ___ to test body sense.
kidTest.explain: Finding your nose with eyes closed uses body position sense.

kidTest.q: The message stops at a relay station in the middle of the brain called the:
kidTest.explain: The thalamus passes messages on to the cortex.

advancedTest.q: Medial medullary infarction on the left produces:
choices: Left face pain loss and Horner
Right body proprioceptive loss, right hemiparesis, left tongue weakness
advancedTest.explain: Left medial medulla damages the left medial lemniscus (already crossed: right body), the left pyramid (uncrossed yet: right body weakness) and the left hypoglossal nerve (left tongue).

advancedTest.q: During scoliosis surgery, SSEPs remain normal but the patient wakes paraplegic. The most likely injured territory is:
advancedTest.explain: SSEPs monitor dorsal columns (posterior circulation of the cord). Anterior spinal artery injury damages corticospinal tracts and anterior horns; motor evoked potentials detect it.

advancedTest.q: Midline myelotomy relieves visceral cancer pain. This supports the existence of:
choices: Pain fibers in the corticospinal tract
A visceral nociceptive pathway in the dorsal columns
advancedTest.explain: The postsynaptic dorsal column pathway carries visceral nociception medially in the dorsal columns.

advancedTest.q: Electric shock sensation down the spine on neck flexion is called what sign?
advancedTest.explain: Lhermitte sign reflects cervical dorsal column irritation, classically in MS.

lessons.title: Pain & Temperature Pathways

levels.kid:
Pain is your body's alarm. It says, "Hey, stop, that could hurt you!"

Pain and hot or cold messages take a different road than touch. They cross to the other side of your spinal cord almost right away, then climb up to your brain.

The messages go to a relay station in the middle of your brain. From there, some go to the part that says WHERE it hurts. Others go to the parts that make you feel upset or scared about it.

That is why pain does not just say "ouch here." It also makes you feel "I don't like this!"
levels.hs:
Pain, temperature and crude touch travel in the **anterolateral system**, mainly the **spinothalamic tract**.

The route:
- **1st neuron**: thin A-delta or C fiber with its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion. It enters the spinal cord and synapses in the **dorsal horn**, often after moving up or down a segment or two in Lissauer's tract.
- **2nd neuron**: in the dorsal horn. Its axon **crosses right away** (within a segment or two) through the anterior white commissure and climbs on the **opposite side** as the lateral spinothalamic tract.
- **3rd neuron**: in the thalamus, projecting to the somatosensory cortex.

Compare this with touch: touch crosses in the medulla, but pain crosses in the spinal cord. So damaging one side of the spinal cord causes loss of pain and temperature on the **opposite** side, but loss of fine touch and position sense on the **same** side. That pattern is called **Brown-Séquard syndrome**.

Pain also travels to brain areas for emotion, like the **insula** and **anterior cingulate cortex**, which is why pain feels unpleasant, not just located.

Face pain uses the trigeminal nerve and the **spinal trigeminal nucleus**, which reaches down into the upper cervical cord.
levels.college:
**Anterolateral system (ALS)**: pain, temperature, itch and crude touch.

- **First-order**: A-delta and C afferents enter via the dorsolateral fasciculus (**Lissauer's tract**) and terminate in the dorsal horn: lamina I (marginal zone), lamina II (substantia gelatinosa, mostly interneurons) and lamina V (wide dynamic range neurons). Transmitters: glutamate, with substance P and CGRP from peptidergic fibers.
- **Second-order**: projection neurons in laminae I and V cross in the **anterior white commissure** within one or two segments and ascend in the contralateral anterolateral funiculus. The tract is somatotopic: sacral fibers lateral, cervical fibers medial.
- **Targets**:
- **Spinothalamic**: to VPL (sensory-discriminative: where, how intense) and to medial/intralaminar thalamus (affective)
- **Spinoreticular**: arousal
- **Spinomesencephalic**: to the periaqueductal gray, engaging descending modulation
- Cortical targets: S1, S2, **insula** and **anterior cingulate cortex**, forming the so-called pain matrix.

**Face**: pain and temperature afferents in the trigeminal nerve descend in the **spinal trigeminal tract** to the spinal trigeminal nucleus (caudal part continuous with the dorsal horn), cross, and ascend to **VPM**.

**Key lesions**:
- **Brown-Séquard**: contralateral pain/temperature loss beginning a level or two below the lesion, ipsilateral DCML loss and weakness below.
- **Syringomyelia**: a central cavity destroys crossing fibers in the anterior commissure, giving bilateral "cape-like" pain/temperature loss over shoulders and arms with preserved touch (dissociated sensory loss).
- **Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome**: ipsilateral face and contralateral body pain/temperature loss.
- **Anterior spinal artery syndrome**: bilateral pain/temperature loss and paralysis below the lesion with preserved dorsal columns.

**Referred pain**: visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same dorsal horn neurons, so cardiac pain is felt in the left arm and jaw.
levels.phd:
**Dorsal horn circuitry.** Lamina I projection neurons are a small minority of dorsal horn cells; most are excitatory and inhibitory interneurons forming transcriptionally defined populations. Lamina I neurons include nociceptive-specific, polymodal (heat-pinch-cold) and thermoreceptive cells, many expressing the NK1 receptor for substance P. Ablating NK1-expressing lamina I neurons in rodents reduces hyperalgesia while sparing acute pain, implying distinct circuits for baseline and sensitized pain.

**Wide dynamic range (WDR) neurons** in lamina V respond to innocuous and noxious stimuli with graded firing and receive convergent visceral input, providing the substrate for referred pain (convergence-projection theory).

**Thalamocortical routes.** Craig proposed a dedicated lamina I to posterior ventromedial nucleus (VMpo) to dorsal posterior insula pathway representing the physiological condition of the body (interoception), distinct from the VPL route to S1. Whether VMpo is a distinct primate nucleus is debated, but the posterior insula is a key site: stimulating it evokes pain, and lesions there can cause asymbolia for pain or central pain.

**Affect and the cingulate.** Rainville's hypnosis studies dissociated pain intensity (S1 activity) from unpleasantness (anterior cingulate activity). Cingulotomy historically reduced the suffering component of intractable pain while patients still reported the sensation.

**The "pain matrix" critique.** Many regions active during pain respond to any salient stimulus, so imaging patterns may reflect salience rather than pain itself. Multivariate signatures (for example the neurologic pain signature) attempt more specific decoding, but none yet substitutes for self-report.

**Itch** shares the anterolateral route but uses distinct spinal circuitry: pruriceptors activate gastrin-releasing peptide receptor (GRPR) interneurons, and inhibitory Bhlhb5-lineage interneurons mediate scratch-induced suppression of itch, a clean example of cross-modal gating.
levels.expert:
**Bedside localization with pain and temperature.** Test pinprick and cold (a cool tuning fork works) and compare with vibration and position.

**Patterns to recognize:**
- **Hemicord (Brown-Séquard)**, often from penetrating trauma, disc or tumor: ipsilateral weakness and lost vibration/proprioception, contralateral lost pinprick starting slightly below the lesion level. Prognosis for walking is relatively good compared with other incomplete cord syndromes.
- **Central cord syndrome**, typically an older patient with cervical spondylosis after a hyperextension injury: arms weaker than legs, variable cape-like sensory loss. Lamination explains the sparing: the lateral (sacral, leg) fibers are farthest from the center.
- **Syringomyelia** with Chiari I malformation: painless burns on the hands, cape-like loss of pinprick, later hand atrophy and areflexia in the arms as the cavity extends into the anterior horns. Treatment often starts with posterior fossa decompression to restore CSF flow.
- **Sacral sparing** of pinprick in an intramedullary lesion; in spinal cord injury, preserved sacral sensation defines an **incomplete** injury (ASIA grade B or better), which carries a much better prognosis.
- **Wallenberg syndrome** (vertebral or PICA occlusion): crossed sensory loss, ipsilateral Horner, hoarseness and dysphagia, vertigo, ipsilateral limb ataxia.

**Neurosurgical pain procedures based on this anatomy:**
- **Anterolateral cordotomy** (now usually percutaneous at C1–C2) lesions the spinothalamic tract and gives contralateral analgesia, used for unilateral cancer pain in patients with limited life expectancy; pain often recurs after months to years, and bilateral high cordotomy risks sleep apnea (Ondine's curse).
- **Trigeminal tractotomy-nucleotomy** targets the descending trigeminal tract for facial pain.

**Pitfall**: referred pain misleads. Shoulder-tip pain may be diaphragmatic irritation (C3–C5 phrenic), and left arm or jaw pain may be cardiac. Always consider the visceral source before blaming a nerve root.

keyPoints: Pain, temperature and crude touch travel in the anterolateral (spinothalamic) system
2nd-order neurons in the dorsal horn cross within 1–2 segments via the anterior white commissure
Spinal hemisection: ipsilateral DCML loss + contralateral pain/temperature loss (Brown-Séquard)
Syringomyelia: bilateral cape-like pain/temperature loss with preserved touch
Face pain uses the spinal trigeminal tract/nucleus → VPM; Wallenberg = ipsilateral face + contralateral body loss

lessons.title: Pain Modulation

levels.kid:
Why do you rub your elbow after you bump it? Because rubbing really helps!

Your spinal cord has little gates. Pain messages have to go through a gate to reach your brain. When you rub the sore spot, touch messages rush in and help close the gate a bit. So less pain gets through.

Your brain can close the gates too. It makes its own natural painkillers. That is why someone playing an exciting game might not notice a scrape until later.

So pain is not just about the hurt. Your body can turn the pain volume up or down!
levels.hs:
Pain is not a simple wire from injury to brain. Signals are **turned up or down** along the way.

**Gate control theory** (Melzack and Wall, 1965): in the dorsal horn, touch fibers (A-beta) activate small inhibitory neurons that dampen pain signals. That is why rubbing a bump or using a TENS unit (mild electrical skin stimulation) can reduce pain.

**Descending control**: the brain sends signals down to the spinal cord to block pain.
- The **periaqueductal gray (PAG)** in the midbrain activates the **rostral ventromedial medulla**, which projects to the dorsal horn.
- These pathways use **serotonin** and **norepinephrine**.
- **Endogenous opioids** (endorphins, enkephalins, dynorphins) act on opioid receptors to block pain transmission.

This explains why soldiers or athletes sometimes do not feel serious injuries until later (stress-induced analgesia), and why placebos can truly reduce pain.

Pain can also be turned **up**:
- **Peripheral sensitization**: inflamed tissue releases chemicals (prostaglandins, bradykinin) that make nociceptors more sensitive. Anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) work by blocking prostaglandin production.
- **Central sensitization**: repeated pain input makes spinal neurons more excitable, so even light touch can hurt.
levels.college:
**Gate control.** Melzack and Wall proposed that substantia gelatinosa interneurons inhibit transmission from nociceptive afferents to projection neurons, and that A-beta input increases this inhibition. Details of the original wiring were wrong, but the core idea of segmental inhibition by large-fiber input survives and underlies TENS and spinal cord stimulation.

**Descending modulation:**
- **PAG** receives input from prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, amygdala and hypothalamus, so expectation, fear and attention shape pain.
- PAG projects to the **rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM)**, including the nucleus raphe magnus. RVM **OFF cells** inhibit and **ON cells** facilitate nociceptive transmission; opioids activate OFF cells and silence ON cells.
- Noradrenergic projections from the **locus coeruleus** inhibit dorsal horn transmission via alpha-2 receptors.
- Reynolds (1969) performed abdominal surgery in rats under PAG stimulation alone: stimulation-produced analgesia.

**Opioid mechanisms.** Endogenous peptides: beta-endorphin (mu), enkephalins (delta), dynorphins (kappa). Opioid receptors are Gi/o-coupled: presynaptically they close voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing transmitter release from nociceptor terminals; postsynaptically they open GIRK potassium channels, hyperpolarizing dorsal horn neurons. Naloxone is a competitive antagonist.

**Facilitation and sensitization:**
- **Peripheral**: the inflammatory soup (bradykinin, PGE2, protons, serotonin, histamine, nerve growth factor) lowers nociceptor thresholds, producing **primary hyperalgesia**. COX inhibitors reduce prostaglandin synthesis.
- **Central**: repetitive C-fiber input causes **wind-up** and long-term potentiation at dorsal horn synapses. Depolarization relieves the magnesium block of **NMDA receptors**, increasing calcium entry and excitability. Results include **secondary hyperalgesia** (around the injury) and **allodynia** (pain from normally innocuous stimuli).

**Placebo analgesia** is partly reversible by naloxone, showing release of endogenous opioids driven by expectation.
levels.phd:
**Bidirectional descending control.** The PAG-RVM system is not just an analgesic circuit but a bidirectional dial. RVM ON cells burst just before nocifensive withdrawal and are activated during opioid withdrawal and in chronic pain models; OFF cells pause before withdrawal and are activated by mu agonists. Persistent descending facilitation from the RVM helps maintain neuropathic pain behavior in rodents, since lesioning the dorsolateral funiculus or ablating mu-receptor-expressing RVM neurons reverses established hypersensitivity.

**Monoamine complexity.** Serotonin can be inhibitory (5-HT1A, 5-HT1B/D, 5-HT7 in some contexts) or facilitatory (5-HT3 on primary afferent terminals). This explains why SSRIs are weak analgesics, whereas drugs raising both serotonin and norepinephrine (SNRIs, tricyclics) work better: spinal alpha-2 adrenergic inhibition is a dominant analgesic mechanism.

**Conditioned pain modulation (diffuse noxious inhibitory controls)**, where pain in one body area inhibits pain elsewhere, depends on a spino-bulbo-spinal loop through the subnucleus reticularis dorsalis. Reduced conditioned pain modulation predicts development of chronic postoperative pain and characterizes fibromyalgia, supporting a model of deficient endogenous inhibition.

**Opioid tolerance and hyperalgesia.** Chronic mu activation causes receptor phosphorylation, beta-arrestin recruitment, internalization and adenylyl cyclase superactivation. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia involves NMDA receptor activation, spinal dynorphin, and microglial signaling via TLR4. Biased mu agonists that favor G protein over beta-arrestin signaling were proposed to separate analgesia from respiratory depression, but the hypothesis has weakened as respiratory depression proved G protein-mediated too.

**Cognitive modulation.** Expectation engages dorsolateral prefrontal and rostral anterior cingulate projections to PAG. Spinal fMRI shows placebo reduces dorsal horn responses, demonstrating top-down modulation at the first synapse. Nocebo effects involve cholecystokinin signaling and can be blocked by CCK antagonists.
levels.expert:
**Multimodal analgesia** is modulation applied deliberately: hit several points in the pathway so no single drug carries the load.

- **Periphery**: NSAIDs and acetaminophen reduce prostaglandin-driven sensitization; local anesthetic infiltration and regional nerve blocks stop transmission at the source.
- **Spinal cord**: neuraxial opioids, and alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, dexmedetomidine).
- **Descending systems**: SNRIs and tricyclics enhance noradrenergic inhibition, useful in chronic and neuropathic pain.
- **Cognitive and behavioral**: expectation, sleep, mood and catastrophizing strongly predict pain; cognitive behavioral therapy and graded activity change outcomes.

Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) pathways in spine surgery combine these to cut opioid exposure, which matters because opioid tolerance, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, constipation, sedation and respiratory depression all worsen recovery. Naloxone reverses opioid respiratory depression; titrate carefully in dependent patients to avoid precipitating severe withdrawal and pain.

**Neuromodulation:**
- **Spinal cord stimulation**: epidural leads over the dorsal columns, originally justified by gate control; used for persistent radicular pain after spine surgery and painful diabetic neuropathy. Newer paradigms (high-frequency, burst, closed-loop) can work without paresthesia, so the mechanism is clearly more than classical gating.
- **Intrathecal drug delivery** pumps for refractory cancer pain or spasticity.
- **Deep brain stimulation** of PAG/periventricular gray or sensory thalamus has a long history for intractable pain, but results are inconsistent and it remains investigational in most settings; motor cortex stimulation is another option for central pain.

**Clinical pitfall**: escalating opioids for pain that keeps getting worse may be feeding opioid-induced hyperalgesia; diffuse pain that spreads beyond the original site with increasing doses is a clue. Reassess the pain mechanism before adding more of the same drug.

keyPoints: Gate control: A-beta touch input activates dorsal horn inhibitory interneurons (why rubbing and TENS help)
PAG → RVM → dorsal horn descending pathway uses serotonin and norepinephrine; locus coeruleus acts via alpha-2
Endogenous opioids: beta-endorphin (mu), enkephalins (delta), dynorphins (kappa)
Opioids reduce presynaptic Ca2+ entry and open postsynaptic K+ channels
Peripheral sensitization by prostaglandins/bradykinin; central sensitization via NMDA receptors (wind-up)
Placebo analgesia is partly opioid-mediated (naloxone-reversible)

test.explain: Depolarization removes the magnesium block of NMDA receptors, increasing calcium entry and excitability.

kidTest.explain: Touch messages help close the pain gate in the spinal cord.

kidTest.explain: Your brain makes natural painkillers like endorphins.

kidTest.explain: The spinal cord has 'gates' that let more or less pain through.

choices: Their brain turned the pain down
kidTest.explain: The brain can turn the pain volume down for a while.

kidTest.q: Your body can turn the pain volume up or ___.
kidTest.explain: Pain can be turned up or down.

kidTest.explain: False: the brain and spinal cord change how much it hurts.

choices: Spinal noradrenergic (alpha-2) inhibition is a key analgesic mechanism, and serotonin alone can be pro- or anti-nociceptive

advancedTest.explain: Chronic opioids can sensitize pain pathways via NMDA, dynorphin and glial mechanisms.

advancedTest.explain: Weak endogenous inhibition predicts chronic pain development.

lessons.title: Neuropathic Pain

levels.kid:
Usually pain is an alarm that something is hurting your body, like a cut.

But sometimes the nerves themselves get hurt or sick. Then the alarm can go off even when nothing is wrong! It is like a smoke alarm beeping when there is no fire.

This is called nerve pain. It can feel like burning, tingling, or little electric zaps. Sometimes even a soft blanket can hurt.

Regular pain medicine often does not work well for nerve pain. Doctors use special medicines that calm down jumpy nerves.
levels.hs:
There are two big kinds of pain.

**Nociceptive pain** comes from actual or threatened tissue damage, like a sprained ankle or a burn. The nerves are working correctly; they are reporting an injury.

**Neuropathic pain** comes from damage or disease of the **nervous system itself**. The alarm system is broken, so it sends pain signals without a matching injury.

Neuropathic pain often feels like:
- burning or freezing
- electric shocks or shooting pain
- pins and needles
- pain from light touch (**allodynia**)
- numbness in the same area, because nerves are damaged

Common causes:
- **Diabetic neuropathy**: burning feet from nerve damage caused by high blood sugar
- **Shingles** leaving behind **postherpetic neuralgia**
- **Trigeminal neuralgia**: brief, severe electric-shock pains in the face
- **Sciatica** from a pinched nerve root
- **Phantom limb pain** after amputation
- Pain after a stroke or spinal cord injury

Treatment is different from regular pain. Ordinary painkillers often work poorly. Doctors use medicines originally made for seizures or depression, like gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine or amitriptyline, which calm overactive nerves or boost the body's own pain-blocking pathways. Some patients need procedures or surgery.
levels.college:
**Definition (IASP)**: neuropathic pain is pain caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system. It is classified as **peripheral** (diabetic polyneuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, radiculopathy, trigeminal neuralgia, nerve injury) or **central** (post-stroke pain, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis).

**Clinical hallmarks**: positive symptoms (spontaneous burning or shooting pain, paresthesia, allodynia, hyperalgesia) coexisting with negative signs (sensory loss) in a neuroanatomically plausible distribution. Screening tools include DN4 and painDETECT.

**Mechanisms:**
- **Ectopic activity**: injured axons and DRG neurons accumulate sodium channels (including Nav1.7, Nav1.8, and re-expressed Nav1.3), generating spontaneous discharges from neuromas and the ganglion.
- **Central sensitization**: persistent input potentiates dorsal horn synapses through NMDA receptors.
- **Disinhibition**: loss or dysfunction of GABAergic and glycinergic interneurons; downregulation of the chloride transporter KCC2 makes GABA less inhibitory.
- **Glial activation**: microglia release BDNF and cytokines after nerve injury.
- **Sympathetically maintained pain** and **cortical reorganization** (phantom limb).

**First-line drugs** (by mechanism, not dosing):
- **Gabapentinoids** (gabapentin, pregabalin): bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing transmitter release.
- **Tricyclic antidepressants** (amitriptyline, nortriptyline) and **SNRIs** (duloxetine): enhance descending noradrenergic inhibition; tricyclics also block sodium channels.
- Topical lidocaine and high-concentration capsaicin for localized pain.

**Trigeminal neuralgia** is a special case: carbamazepine (a sodium channel blocker) is first-line, and the cause is often vascular compression of the trigeminal root, which is surgically treatable.

Opioids are generally not first-line for chronic neuropathic pain.
levels.phd:
**Mechanism-based classification.** Neuropathic pain trials have high placebo responses and modest effect sizes, partly because diverse mechanisms hide under the same diagnosis. Baron and colleagues proposed sensory phenotyping by quantitative sensory testing: an "irritable nociceptor" phenotype (preserved small-fiber function, heat hyperalgesia) versus a "deafferentation" phenotype (sensory loss). In a randomized trial, oxcarbazepine worked better in patients with the irritable nociceptor phenotype, supporting stratified treatment.

**Peripheral drivers.** Nav1.7 gain-of-function variants are found in a subset of patients with idiopathic small-fiber neuropathy, linking channelopathy to acquired-looking disease. DRG macrophages and satellite glia sustain ectopic firing. Spontaneous activity in C fibers recorded by microneurography in patients correlates with ongoing pain.

**Spinal mechanisms.** After peripheral nerve injury, microglia upregulate the ATP receptor P2X4 and release BDNF, which downregulates KCC2 in lamina I neurons. Intracellular chloride rises, so GABA-A activation becomes less hyperpolarizing or even depolarizing. This converts inhibitory gating into excitation, letting A-beta input reach nociceptive projection neurons and producing tactile allodynia. Loss of dorsal horn PKC-gamma interneuron gating opens similar low-threshold-to-nociceptive routes.

**Central pain.** Central post-stroke pain follows lesions of the spinothalamic system, most often in the thalamus (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome) or lateral medulla. The key requirement is spinothalamic damage; thalamic hyperexcitability and burst firing via T-type calcium channels are proposed mechanisms.

**Phantom limb pain.** Flor linked pain severity to cortical map reorganization, but Makin and colleagues found that the missing hand's representation is largely preserved, and that pain correlates with persistent representation. The causal role of reorganization is therefore disputed, and peripheral DRG activity contributes: DRG anesthesia can abolish phantom pain in some amputees.
levels.expert:
**Diagnosis.** Neuropathic pain needs a plausible lesion and a matching distribution: history plus sensory signs in that territory, confirmed by a test (imaging, nerve conduction, skin biopsy) where possible. Map allodynia and sensory loss on the skin; the overlap of positive and negative signs is the clinical fingerprint.

**Trigeminal neuralgia**, the neurosurgeon's classic:
- Brief, electric-shock pains in V2 and/or V3, triggered by chewing, talking, brushing teeth, or a breeze; the patient is often pain-free between attacks.
- Classical type: **neurovascular compression** of the trigeminal root entry zone, most often by the **superior cerebellar artery**, causing focal demyelination and ephaptic transmission. Secondary causes: multiple sclerosis plaque, tumor (MRI with thin-cut sequences is mandatory). Bilateral or young-onset disease should make you think of MS.
- Medical: carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine first; watch for hyponatremia, rash, and the HLA-B*15:02 association with Stevens-Johnson syndrome in some Asian ancestries.
- Surgical: **microvascular decompression** (Jannetta; retrosigmoid craniotomy, Teflon between artery and nerve) offers the most durable relief in fit patients, with risks including hearing loss and CSF leak. Ablative options for older or high-risk patients: percutaneous balloon compression, glycerol or radiofrequency rhizotomy, and **stereotactic radiosurgery**; these trade durability and facial numbness against invasiveness.

**Other neurosurgical options:**
- **Spinal cord stimulation** for persistent radicular pain after spine surgery and painful diabetic neuropathy; **DRG stimulation** for focal pain such as groin pain or CRPS of the lower limb.
- **DREZ lesioning** (dorsal root entry zone) for brachial plexus avulsion pain, one of its best indications.
- Peripheral nerve surgery for neuromas.

**CRPS**: regional pain out of proportion with swelling, color and temperature changes, sweating and motor changes; type II follows a definable nerve injury. Early mobilization and physiotherapy are central.

**Pitfall**: don't operate on imaging alone. Neurovascular contact is common in pain-free people; the story must be classic.

keyPoints: Neuropathic pain = pain from a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system (IASP)
Features: burning, shooting, electric pain, allodynia, plus sensory loss in the same territory
Mechanisms: ectopic Na+ channel firing, central sensitization, disinhibition (KCC2 loss), microglial activation
First-line drug classes: gabapentinoids (alpha-2-delta), tricyclics, SNRIs; topical lidocaine/capsaicin for focal pain
Trigeminal neuralgia: often superior cerebellar artery compression; carbamazepine first; microvascular decompression is most durable
Central pain follows spinothalamic damage, e.g., thalamic stroke (Dejerine-Roussy)
